name: legacy-passwords
documentation: Verify a password against a hash some OTHER system wrote, so users can be migrated without being asked to reset. Nine schemes: bcrypt, Argon2, crypt(3) (md5/sha256/sha512), phpass ($P$ and $H$), Django PBKDF2, RFC 7914 scrypt (pure PHP — no extension), Firebase's modified scrypt, salted or unsalted digests, and plaintext. Every one is pinned by a known-answer test whose expected value came from a DIFFERENT implementation. No database table, no migration, no routes.
//the-only-flow: A legacy hash can only ever be replaced DURING A LOGIN, because that is the only moment the plaintext exists. There is no batch job that can re-hash a password table — not for these schemes, not for bcrypt, not for any scheme ever designed. So the flow is: verify the old hash, and in the same request write a new one with the application's own HashingPort. LegacyVerdict::mustUpgrade() is true for every success for exactly that reason, and skipping it means paying the legacy cost on every future login forever.
//why-not-in-crypto: crypto.services owns HashingPort and would have been the convenient home. It was rejected because EVERY project loads crypto.services — it is how passwords are hashed — so putting MD5, unsalted SHA and plaintext verification there would make every application everywhere carry code that can check a password against an unsalted MD5, and would force a security review of the hashing plugin to reason about nine deliberately weak schemes it never uses. Here they live in a module a project loads only if it is migrating off something.
//no-routes-is-a-security-decision: POST /legacy/verify taking a password and a hash is an ORACLE: it tests arbitrary passwords against arbitrary hashes at the server's expense. That is a password-cracking service, and at a measured 1.58 seconds per scrypt call it is also a denial of service with a one-line request. The capability is a service method and the application decides who may call it.
//no-algorithm-guessing: There is no 'try them all' mode and there will not be one. Verifying a 32-character hex digest against md5(pw), then md5(salt.pw), then md5(pw.salt) gives an attacker four chances at a collision instead of one, and a collision in the WEAKEST scheme on the list authenticates a user whose password was stored under the strongest — the security of the set becomes the security of its worst member. Self-describing hashes ($2y$, $argon2id$, $1$/$5$/$6$, $P$/$H$, pbkdf2_*) are detected by unambiguous prefix. Bare digests are DECLARED, by whoever read the source application's code and therefore actually knows.
//what-appwrite-cannot-read: Appwrite's md5 and sha importers hash the password and nothing else — md5($value), hash('sha256', $value) — so a SALTED digest column, which is the overwhelming majority of real legacy tables, has no path through them. Its scrypt and scryptMod importers both require the ext-scrypt PECL extension and throw 'The scrypt extension is required' without it, so on a stock PHP they cannot run at all. This plugin's salt placement, salt encoding and pure-PHP scrypt exist to close exactly those gaps.
//deliberately-absent: Drupal 7 ($S$) and MySQL's PASSWORD() (*HEX40) are both real and both commonly met in an import, and both are ABSENT for one reason: nothing on the machine this was written on could say whether an implementation of them was correct. Every scheme that IS here is pinned against a second implementation — Python's and Node's scrypt, Node's AES-256-CTR, Python's hashlib, openssl passwd, a separate PHP phpass, PHP's own password_hash. For those two the only option left would have been to write the algorithm from memory and let the test assert whatever the code happened to produce: a test that cannot fail, guarding a path that gates logging in. The constructions are recorded in the README, and adding either needs one real hash of a known password. libsodium's $7$ is also absent, because a system new enough to use libsodium's password API is not one this plugin exists to migrate off.
//plaintext-is-off-by-default: A plaintext password column is a real thing real schemas have, and refusing to read one does not make those passwords safer — it makes migrating off them harder, which is the opposite of the goal. So it is supported, and refused unless LEGACY_PASSWORD_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT is turned on deliberately, with a date on the decision.
//why-cost-ceilings: A self-describing hash carries its own work factor, and an import file from the system being migrated away from is not trusted input. One row containing $2y$31$… is a valid bcrypt hash with 2^31 rounds — hours of CPU for one verification — so from then on every login attempt against that account occupies a PHP worker until the request times out. A handful of such rows is a denial of service that needs no traffic to trigger. The ceilings turn that into a refusal with a reason, and are generous enough that nothing met in practice comes near them.
//kernel-floor: ^1.3.3 is the MEASURED minimum rather than the current release. HashingPort dates from v1.0.0 and so do CliPipeline::defer() and command(instance); LoggerPort is what sets the floor at 1.3.3. Established with `git log -S` plus `git tag --contains` in the kernel, not guessed.
